title: When more is not enough
lines: What if abundance makes a civilization's appetite faster, without making it satisfied?
Wendigo asks why greater capability does not automatically teach us when to stop.
This is a philosophical systems argument, not a supernatural horror story.
It connects cultural images of hunger with competition, institutions and technological power.
The practical question is how a society can preserve the conditions it depends on.
You are invited to examine the difference between meeting needs and extending appetite.
That distinction gives the book its purpose, and its uncomfortable force.

title: A name with boundaries
lines: The book begins by placing a limit on its own use of mythology.
Its title draws from living Indigenous traditions that are neither interchangeable nor decorative.
The introduction explains why a generic antlered forest monster would miss the point.
The relevant connection concerns hunger, reciprocity and obligations that support communal survival.
The author develops a narrower systems hypothesis from that encounter.
The traditions do not become scientific evidence merely because their images are powerful.
Reading begins with that distinction, which governs the rest of the argument.

One person's excess can reduce the margin protecting someone else's next meal.

The frightening feature is appetite that has lost its relation to other lives.
The book then asks what changes when institutions reward the fastest consumer.
A restrained participant may lose position even while restraint would help the group.
The problem moves from private character toward the rules selecting public behavior.

title: Desire and craving
lines: The hungry ghost introduces a different problem from simply lacking enough food.
Consumption itself may fail to complete the act of satisfaction.
The book distinguishes useful aspiration from craving that continually recreates dissatisfaction.
Learning, care and escape from deprivation still require desires worth pursuing.
Its criticism is therefore not a demand that people stop wanting better lives.
It asks how a valuable aim changes when it has no stopping condition.
That question can apply even to aims we ordinarily regard as good.

title: A product without an ending
lines: The chapter on manufactured hunger brings the argument into familiar interfaces.
A system can answer a need, or continually make another desire salient.
Recommendations observe behavior and then help shape the environment producing that behavior.
The author treats this as a feedback loop, not literal mind control.
Personalization can help people while incentives still reward keeping them engaged.
A useful question follows about whether products can succeed when their users finish.
The book makes that an institutional design issue rather than a private lifestyle test.

title: What limits make possible
lines: The biological chapters ask what prevents local advantage from damaging a larger system.
Multicellular life depends on constraints that make specialized cooperation possible.
The author uses cancer as a carefully bounded analogy about those constraints failing.
Cells are not moral agents, and societies are not literally bodies.
The text explicitly rejects applying the analogy to peoples or political enemies.
Its narrower question concerns mechanisms that keep successful parts from consuming shared conditions.
Those qualifications are part of the argument, not optional cautions around its edges.

title: Who carries the cost
lines: An apparently successful decision can place its costs outside the decision-maker's account.
The book follows that displacement toward people with less power to refuse.
Aggregate abundance does not establish that everyone can access food, care or shelter.
Nor does finding waste prove that every shortage has a simple logistical remedy.
The argument requires attention to distribution, institutions and the location of risk.
This makes its critique more demanding than saying that consumption is always bad.
It asks whose missing options are paying for somebody else's visible improvement.

title: Which limits deserve respect
lines: A defense of limits must confront the history of unjust limits.
The book acknowledges that taboos have protected oppression as well as vulnerable goods.
It therefore does not propose restoring every inherited prohibition.
Instead, it asks readers to distinguish false barriers from protective boundaries.
Some constraints can move through invention, while others preserve agency or shared resilience.
That diagnosis needs evidence, criticism and a credible possibility of revision.
The value of reading lies in learning to make the distinctions together.

title: The absent party
lines: Future people cannot negotiate many of the commitments being made in their name.
The book treats that absence as a structural temptation for present institutions.
Building for tomorrow can be beneficial, so borrowing from the future is not inherently wrong.
The question is what inheritance accompanies the obligations and depleted options.
Reversibility matters because some experiments permit correction while others close possibilities for everyone.
The author asks for stronger restraint as irreversible exposure widens.
The chapter develops that judgment without claiming an exact date for a civilization's collapse.

title: Capability needs judgment
lines: The book takes the promise of technological abundance seriously, including cheaper intelligence.
It also asks whether cheaper capability can make unsatisfied appetite more effective.
Relative status and control do not disappear simply because material production improves.
Nor does greater technical ability automatically supply legitimacy for its use.
Judgment can become a tighter bottleneck as actions become easier to produce.
This is where the discussion connects economic incentives to technological governance.
The question is what greater power requires from the institutions directing it.

title: The wisdom of brakes
lines: A brake preserves possibilities by refusing part of the momentum available now.
The final chapters use that image to make restraint into collective technology.
Safety margins, independent checks and credible stopping conditions all have real costs.
Private moderation cannot by itself solve a competition that punishes the moderate participant.
Rules and coordination must make restraint possible without handing unlimited power to gatekeepers.
The book also insists that those with greater power carry greater obligations.
Its proposal deserves examination precisely where protection, freedom and unequal needs come into tension.

title: Four connected movements
lines: The book moves through mythic images, biological cooperation, forbidden lines and technological futures.
The myths make the pattern memorable, while later chapters test the analogy's usefulness.
The endnote states the central claim as a systems hypothesis, not a diagnosis.
That structure lets you examine both the emotional image and its explanatory limits.
You can disagree with a comparison without losing the question it helps formulate.
The detailed chapters supply qualifications that a striking title cannot carry alone.
Readers gain a vocabulary for judging expansion without treating every improvement as suspect.

title: Read for the distinction
lines: Begin with A Monster Is a Model to understand the book's interpretive contract.
Then read The Winter Cannibal alongside The Wisdom of Brakes.
Ask how an individual temptation becomes a competitive rule that resists correction.
Keep testing whether a boundary protects people or merely protects its own authority.
The book gives that question more room than a simple warning against excess.
Its strongest invitation is to examine where your preferred good needs a stopping condition.
Read Wendigo for the argument behind that uncomfortable word, enough.
